case_study_insert.main_stem: Gransden Fasteners (GDF) is a private limited company in the precision fasteners and fixings manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 1998 by Lebo Gransden in Durban, the business supplies certified bolts and fixings to construction and furniture makers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. GDF plans to invest $750,000 in a new cold-heading fastener line, financed by a $500,000 five-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit after a share issue was rejected. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. GDF faces skilled labour turnover and a training gap on the new cold-heading machines.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The fastener line produced 20,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 1.6%, down from 2.8% a year ago, and received 12 customer returns per month. Average delivery time is 6 days. A survey of 350 hardware distributors found that 61% buy mainly on price, while 44% value certified strength markings. A skills audit shows 10 of 50 operators lack on-the-job training on the new cold-heading machines; off-the-job training at the engineering college costs $850 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Gransden Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 7.0% to 7.8%, increasing debt-service costs for leveraged manufacturers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $10.50 to $11.26 per hour from April 2026. (3) Imported steel wire rod and coating Input costs have risen 13.4% year-on-year, while diesel and transport fuel is up 8.1%, raising delivery expenses.

questions.question_text: GDF rejected a share issue and instead borrowed $500,000 for its $750,000 cold-heading line. Explain two advantages for GDF of using this bank loan rather than a share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bank loan leaves ownership and control with Lebo Gransden and the existing shareholders, so the flat structure and laissez-faire style are preserved without new investors demanding dividends or a say in decisions. The $500,000 is repaid on known terms alongside the $250,000 retained profit, unlike equity where the cost of a share issue is permanent dilution, which matters when 61% of the 350 surveyed distributors buy mainly on price and GDF needs to stay focused on cost.

Point 2: Borrowing is quicker and more confidential than a share issue for a private limited company, allowing the $750,000 cold-heading machines to be ordered without a lengthy investor process, and interest payments reduce taxable profit. Provided the 80,000-unit output and $15.00 selling price generate enough contribution, the loan can be serviced from trading cash flow while keeping the 44% of distributors who value certified strength markings supplied without the pressure to distribute profits to new shareholders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to GDF's loan, ownership and expansion.

questions.question_text: GDF is promoting its new certified fastener range. Consider listings in trade directories, a direct-mail catalogue to hardware distributors, or exhibiting at a construction trade show. Which should GDF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade directory listings: Being listed in engineering and construction directories gives GDF a permanent, low-cost presence where buyers already search for certified bolts, and supports the 44% of 350 distributors who value strength markings. However, a listing is passive, offers little room to demonstrate certification, and with 61% buying on price GDF risks being compared only on cost, so enquiries may be weak.

Direct-mail catalogue: A printed catalogue posted to hardware distributors can show the full fastener range, price list and certification details, and can be targeted at the exact 350-surveyor segment with measurable responses. The drawbacks are printing and postage costs, low response rates, and the risk that a static price list reinforces the 61% price-first mindset rather than the quality message GDF wants for its new line.

Construction trade show: An exhibition lets buyers handle samples and meet GDF engineers, making certification tangible and generating immediate orders, but stands, travel and staff time are expensive for a firm funding a $750,000 line with a $500,000 loan, and it reaches only attendees within a short window.

Recommendation: GDF should choose the direct-mail catalogue as its main channel, supported by a basic directory listing. The catalogue can be targeted and measured, explains the certified strength marking to the 44% who value it, and is cheaper than a trade show; the directory listing adds low-cost year-round presence. A full trade-show stand is rejected as too costly and time-limited given the loan commitment and a 6-day delivery promise that must be protected.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GDF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GDF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the other two are secondary.

questions.question_text: GDF has a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership but faces skilled labour turnover. Explain two benefits for GDF of introducing team working among its 50 operators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the 50 operators share knowledge about the cold-heading machines, so the 10 workers lacking on-the-job training can learn from experienced colleagues while output of 80,000 units continues. This supports the flat structure, reduces the isolation that laissez-faire leadership can create, and helps cut the 1.6% defect rate as teams collectively spot faults, protecting the 44% of distributors who value certified strength markings.

Point 2: Giving teams responsibility for their own area can raise commitment and reduce the skilled labour turnover that GDF faces, because operators feel their ideas are used rather than ignored under a hands-off style. Retaining skilled workers avoids repeated off-the-job training at $850 per employee and maintains the 6-day delivery time, ensuring the $750,000 investment is operated by experienced staff who can sustain quality as the new line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GDF's turnover, training gap and structure.

questions.question_text: GDF must train 10 of its 50 operators on the new cold-heading machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the engineering college. Which should GDF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the cold-heading machines is specific to GDF's own processes and the 1.6% defect target, costs no fees and keeps the 10 operators producing fasteners while they learn, protecting the 20,000 units made last quarter and the 6-day delivery time. Its limits are that trainers lose output, bad habits may be copied, and no certificate is awarded, which is a concern because 44% of distributors value certified strength markings.

Off-the-job training: The engineering college course at $850 per employee costs $8,500 for 10 operators, modest against the $750,000 line, and provides structured skills and a recognised credential that reinforces GDF's certified quality message. It removes 10 of 50 staff from production, however, slowing output when labour turnover is already a problem, and generic content may not match GDF's exact machine settings without later coaching.

Decision: GDF should choose on-the-job training first, with short college modules for supervisors. It is cheapest, machine-specific and protects the 6-day delivery and 1.6% defect performance while turnover is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 10 of 50 operators and spending $8,500 would disrupt supply to price-sensitive distributors, and certification can be added once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GDF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of GDF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in context with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GDF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($15.00 − $6.00) = $216,000 ÷ $9.00 = 24,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 24,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 − $6.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GDF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 24,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units, a margin of safety of 56,000 units, to judge whether the $750,000 cold-heading line can safely be run at full capacity.
2. Use the $9.00 contribution per unit to assess the 61% of distributors who buy on price: managers can model a small price cut and see how many extra units are needed to keep covering the $216,000 fixed costs.
3. Set the volume needed to service the $500,000 bank loan from contribution, checking the new line earns enough before GDF commits to more capital spending.
4. Track unit cost ($216,000 ÷ 80,000 units + $6.00 = $8.70) each quarter to detect waste behind the 1.6% defect rate and the 13.4% steel wire rod inflation, guiding supplier negotiations and the 6-day delivery promise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 24,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 56,000 units vs 80,000 output; price-cut modelling at $9.00 contribution; loan-service volume for the $750,000 line; and unit-cost tracking at $8.70 to cut 1.6% defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GDF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GDF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.92 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $260,000; 2025 current assets = $105,000 + $110,000 + $55,000 = $270,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $260,000 ÷ $200,000 and 2025 $270,000 ÷ $180,000. Excluding inventories, liquid assets are 2024 ($260,000 − $90,000) = $170,000 and 2025 ($270,000 − $105,000) = $165,000, divided by the same current liabilities to give the four figures stated above.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved but remains modest. The first measure rose from 1.30 to 1.50 because current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $180,000 while current assets increased, so short-term debts are more comfortably covered. The second measure, which removes stock, improved from 0.85 to 0.92, yet both are still below 1.0, meaning GDF would need to sell inventories or receive customer payments before it could cover all current obligations — a concern while it services a $500,000 loan and a $750,000 investment. Trade receivables did fall from $130,000 to $110,000 and cash rose from $40,000 to $55,000, which is helpful, but inventories grew to $105,000, so more cash is tied up in fastener stock and the 6-day delivery promise depends on that stock being available.

Conclusion: GDF's financial position has improved, but only modestly. Both liquidity measures moved favourably (1.30 to 1.50 and 0.85 to 0.92), yet the second stays under 1.0, so the improvement is not yet robust; tighter stock and credit management would strengthen it before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GDF of introducing a steel offcut recycling scheme to reduce waste.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycling steel offcuts from the cold-heading process can cut material waste and lower the $6.00 variable cost per unit, helping GDF compete with the 61% of distributors who buy mainly on price while protecting the $9.00 contribution that services the $500,000 loan. It also supports the certified quality image valued by 44% of buyers and reduces disposal costs at a time when steel wire rod inflation is 13.4%.

Disadvantage: Installing collection and baling equipment requires spending beyond the $750,000 already committed, and organising segregation takes time from the 50 operators, who already have a training gap and a 1.6% defect rate to manage. If recycled material is of inconsistent quality, it could raise defects above 1.6% and trigger more than the current 12 customer returns per month, undermining the certified strength marking that 44% of distributors value and lengthening the 6-day delivery time.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GDF's costs, waste and market research.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 7.8%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 13.4% rise in steel wire rod costs will affect GDF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (7.0% to 7.8%): If GDF's $500,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.8% of $500,000 = $4,000 a year (0.008 × $500,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $216,000, and a fixed-rate loan would see no direct rise. Higher rates may make price-sensitive construction and furniture customers cut orders and raise the cost of future funding, but GDF can cap the damage by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $11.26 per hour): With a workforce of 50, some packing and support roles are likely hourly-paid, so this raises the wage bill unavoidably. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the reliable comparison is with the given productivity of 80,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,600 units per worker. Unless that productivity is held or output rises, unit labour cost increases and the $9.00 contribution per unit is squeezed, while labour turnover remains a concern.

Steel wire rod input inflation (13.4%): GDF's variable cost of $6.00 per unit includes steel, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an explicitly labelled bound is defensible: if the full $6.00 rose 13.4% it would add 13.4% × $6.00 = $0.80 per unit, about $64,000 a year at 80,000 units, pulling contribution from $9.00 toward $8.20. Because 61% of distributors buy mainly on price, passing this on is difficult, so margin absorption is likely.

Conclusion: The 13.4% steel wire rod rise will have the greatest impact because it hits every fastener in the 80,000-unit output and directly erodes the $9.00 contribution that supports the $750,000 investment, with little pricing power given price-first buyers. The loan increase is only $4,000 a year and the wage effect depends on unstated hours and can be offset by 1,600-unit productivity, so both are smaller or less certain.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GDF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GDF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
